\section[\ar{عفوا}]{\ar{عفوا} (ʿafwan) — "you're welcome," from a root meaning "to erase"}

\label{lesson:AR-C23-afwan}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Your very first Arabic lesson already used this word once, in passing, as the reply to \emph{shukran}. Here it gets its own full treatment — starting with a root that literally means "to erase."
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{عفوا}} (\emph{ʿafwan}), root \textbf{ʿ-f-w} (\textbf{\ar{ع}-\ar{ف}-\ar{و}}): the root's core sense is "\textbf{to erase, obliterate, remove}" — and "to pardon, forgive" grows directly out of that, since forgiving something is, metaphorically, \textbf{erasing} it. The same root gives \textbf{\ar{العفو}} (\emph{al-ʿAfuww}, "\textbf{the Supreme Pardoner}"), one of the \textbf{99 names of Allah} in Islamic tradition.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — Be honest: ʿafwan does more than one job}
\textbf{ʿAfwan} answers \emph{shukran} as "\textbf{you're welcome}" — but depending on tone and context, the exact same word also does duty as "\textbf{excuse me}," "\textbf{pardon}," or "\textbf{sorry}." One root, one word, several closely related jobs — all growing from that same "erase/pardon" sense.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the same ending as shukran itself}]
Look closely at the spelling: \textbf{\ar{عفوا}} ends in the same \textbf{tanwīn fatḥ} ("\textbf{-an}") you already met in \textbf{\ar{شكرا}} (\emph{shukran}) — the indefinite accusative ending. Neither word is a full sentence with its own verb; both are fixed, idiomatic accusative forms functioning as a complete conversational turn on their own. The grammar you learned once, for \emph{shukran}, already explains \emph{ʿafwan} too.
\end{grammarlens}
